title: Why 10x patterns show up everywhere in startups: pricing, people, channels, products
summary: Jason Cohen argues that a "10x rule" is a useful default assumption across startups. Best products, channels, people, products-in-a-portfolio and decisions tend to outperform the rest by roughly 10x, so you should hunt for the one 10x truth instead of fiddling with a hundred variables.

principles.text: Assume a 10x truth exists in your business and spend your time finding it, rather than tuning many minor variables.
principles.quote: it's useful to assume there is a 10x truth, and spend your time seeking that truth, rather than worrying about and fiddling with one hundred variables, almost none of which will turn out to be important.

principles.text: Winning products need at least one attribute that is 10x better than all competitors.
principles.quote: Winning products have at least one attribute that's 10x better than all competitors (and it's not necessarily design, though it can be).

principles.text: Your best marketing channel is often about 10x as productive as the next best, so concentrate on one.
principles.quote: Your best marketing channel is often 10x the productivity of the next-best. True of content-marketing also.

principles.text: SaaS markets follow a power law: the winner can take 10x the profits of the runner-up.
principles.quote: SaaS returns in a market are a power law; winner can take 10x the profits of the next.

principles.text: Companies don't naturally grow 10x in size or quality; it takes intentional focus and investment.
principles.quote: Companies do not naturally 10x their size or quality; that achievement requires intentional focus and investment.

principles.text: In a multi-product company, one product often outearns all the others combined; one or two decisions matter more than the rest together.
principles.quote: For multi-product companies, often one product generates more revenue than all the rest combined.
